paper_metadata.title: Constraint-Aware Quantum Optimization via Hamming Weight Operators

summary: The paper proposes Adaptive Hamming Weight Operator QAOA (AHWO-QAOA), a constraint-preserving QAOA variant, and evaluates it by simulation on portfolio optimization and two-jet clustering instances from 6 to 20 qubits. It reports that AHWO-QAOA satisfies constraints by construction, converges faster, and uses roughly half the gates of penalty-based QAOA at 20 qubits (e.g., about 470 gates vs about 1270 gates in the two-jet benchmark), but no real-hardware or classical-advantage demonstration is provided.

experiments.description: Adaptive Hamming Weight Operator QAOA (AHWO-QAOA) evaluated on portfolio optimization instances with linear budget constraints, compared against penalty-based QAOA baselines.

algorithm.variant: Adaptive Hamming Weight Operator QAOA (AHWO-QAOA); full-parameter / multi-angle QAOA formulation
algorithm.ansatz: Alternating cost Hamiltonian and constraint-preserving mixer layers; adaptive operator-pool ansatz
algorithm.convergence_criteria: until convergence; no explicit numerical stopping rule reported

hyperparameters.approximation_ratio_definition: 1 - |<Hc> - E0| / |E0|; set to 0 whenever constraint violated
hyperparameters.constraint_ratio: fraction of test cases satisfying linear constraints

algorithm.parameter_initialization: variational parameters gamma and beta initialized uniformly at random in (-0.1, 0.1)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 1 qubit per binary decision variable xi in {0,1}
problem_formulation.objective_function: min_x f(x) = sum_{i,j} mu_ij x_i x_j + sum_k eta_k x_k subject to sum_i omega_i x_i = b
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: constraint-preserving Hamming Weight Operators in the mixer; compared against penalty terms in baseline QAOA
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Hc = 1/4 sum_{i,j} mu_ij (1 - sigma_i^z)(1 - sigma_j^z) + 1/2 sum_k eta_k (1 - sigma_k^z)

problem_instance.description: Randomly generated constrained portfolio optimization instances

dataset_specification.description: random coefficients mu_ij and eta_k; random linear constraints consistent with the model

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 100 independent random instances per qubit size; 100 random initializations for convergence analysis

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: random instance generation; construction of operator pool from linear constraints
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: compute approximation ratio and constraint ratio from measured expectation values

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: faster convergence with smaller fluctuations than penalty-based QAOA

speedup_claims.conditions: at 20 qubits; AHWO-QAOA with 1 layer compared against penalty-based QAOA with 5 layers
speedup_claims.caveats: Exact gate counts are not tabulated in the text; the paper states AHWO-QAOA uses approximately half as many gates.
The paper reports qualitative faster convergence and lower variance; only baseline iteration counts are explicitly given in text.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(n) operators in the sparse connectivity-preserving mixer; operator construction via prefix-based search worst-case O(n^2)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: not explicitly characterized for the benchmark optimization problem

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: not established; simulations only up to 20 qubits
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Shallower AHWO-QAOA circuits and roughly half the gate count of 5-layer penalty-based QAOA at 20 qubits; no hardware execution or end-to-end runtime advantage shown
limiting_factors: comparison is against penalty-based QAOA baselines rather than strong classical optimization solvers

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper reports only numerical simulations and no real QPU or noisy simulator device.
Qubit counts, layer counts, and gate-count comparison are explicitly reported in the portfolio optimization section and figure captions.
No explicit classical optimizer name, transpilation details, or shot count are reported.
Authors report better approximation ratio, constraint satisfaction, convergence, and gate counts versus penalty-based QAOA, but do not demonstrate practical quantum advantage over classical methods.
